03 – Explore the CausalCCC authors’ files (case study 2)

Fibroblasts, dendritic cells and T cells in atopic dermatitis skin, CellChat L-R pairs

Author

Minh Le, Jeanne Leclerc

Published

October 8, 2026

Goal

This notebook does for case study 2 (Figure 3 and Supplementary Figure S1 of the paper) what notebook 01 did for case study 1. The files were downloaded by scripts/case2/download_case2.sh from the web server job w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa (sources in data/README.md). We want to understand:

  1. what the authors gave CausalCCC: the mosaic table, the variable list, the L-R pairs, the settings;
  2. what CausalCCC returned;
  3. whether the network supports what the paper says about Figure 3.

The new feature of this case study is that there are three cell types, and each one is both a sender and a receiver. The table also contains metadata (cell subtype and skin condition) as extra variables.

This notebook only reads files: nothing in data/ is modified and nothing is written.

Setup

The helper functions used in notebooks 01 and 02 (find_repo_root(), neighbors_of(), graph_distance(), …) are now in scripts/helpers.R, so that every notebook uses the same version. We load them with source().

library(tidyverse)

# find_repo_root() is needed before we know where helpers.R is, so this short loop is repeated here
root <- getwd()
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))) {
  if (dirname(root) == root) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
  root <- dirname(root)
}
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))

job_dir <- file.path(root, "data", "case2", "causalccc_server_w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa")
if (!dir.exists(job_dir)) stop("Data not found: run scripts/case2/download_case2.sh first.")

1. Read the files

The same files as in case study 1. guess_max = Inf tells read_tsv() to look at every row before deciding the type of a column: the metadata columns are empty (NA) for thousands of rows before their first value, and without this option they would be read as logical columns.

mosaic      <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "input.tsv"), guess_max = Inf, show_col_types = FALSE)
state_order <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_state_order.tsv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
lr_pairs    <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_interact_edges.tsv"),
                        col_names = c("ligand", "receptor"), show_col_types = FALSE)
edges       <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt"), show_col_types = FALSE)
run_log     <- read_lines(file.path(job_dir, "whole_run.log"))

tibble(
  table   = c("mosaic", "state_order", "lr_pairs", "edges"),
  rows    = c(nrow(mosaic), nrow(state_order), nrow(lr_pairs), nrow(edges)),
  columns = c(ncol(mosaic), ncol(state_order), ncol(lr_pairs), ncol(edges))
)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  table        rows columns
  <chr>       <int>   <int>
1 mosaic       7563     238
2 state_order   238       6
3 lr_pairs       43       2
4 edges        8458      17

The mosaic table is byte-for-byte identical to data/case_study2/input.tsv, the copy found online at the start of the project (same md5 checksum, checked when downloading).

2. How the server ran

run_log |>
  str_subset("^Rscript") |>
  str_replace_all(" (--?[a-z])", "\n  \\1") |>
  cat()

  -o /home/miic/server/server_outputs/w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa

The settings are those of case study 1 (see notebook 02, section 2, for the meaning of each option), with one exception: --n_threads 1 instead of 2. The time stamps of the log give the running time on the server:

run_log |>
  str_subset("START miic|Search for conditional|confidence cut|Done!") |>
  str_trunc(110) |>
  cat(sep = "\n")
01/21/2025 01:12:30 PM  R : # -> START miic...
01/21/2025 02:00:26 PM  R : Search for conditional independence relations...
01/21/2025 04:06:41 PM  R : Compute confidence cut with permutations...72 edges cut.
01/21/2025 04:11:29 PM Done!

About three hours, most of it spent searching for conditional independences. The confidence filter removed 72 links.

3. The mosaic table

Each row is a cell of one of the three types. The metadata columns labels_<type> (cell subtype) are filled only for the cells of that type, so they tell us the type of each row. Then, as in notebook 01, the type of a column is the type of the rows where it has values.

cell_types <- c("Fibroblasts", "T_cell", "DCs")

row_type <- case_when(!is.na(mosaic$labels_Fibroblasts) ~ "Fibroblasts",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_T_cell)      ~ "T_cell",
                      !is.na(mosaic$labels_DCs)         ~ "DCs")

col_type <- column_cell_type(mosaic, row_type)

tibble(cell_type = cell_types,
       cells     = map_int(cell_types, \(t) sum(row_type == t, na.rm = TRUE)),
       variables = map_int(cell_types, \(t) sum(col_type == t)))
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cell_type   cells variables
  <chr>       <int>     <int>
1 Fibroblasts  4734        80
2 T_cell       2200        71
3 DCs           629        87
# Every row has a type, and every column belongs to exactly one type?
c(rows_without_type = sum(is.na(row_type)), columns_shared = sum(!col_type %in% cell_types))
rows_without_type    columns_shared 
                0                 0

Is the mosaic exactly made of three filled blocks? For each cell type we check that its rows are complete in its own columns and empty everywhere else.

map(cell_types, \(t) {
  own_rows <- row_type == t
  own_cols <- col_type == t
  tibble(cell_type          = t,
         own_block_complete = !anyNA(mosaic[own_rows, own_cols]),
         elsewhere_empty    = all(is.na(mosaic[own_rows, !own_cols])))
}) |> list_rbind()
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  cell_type   own_block_complete elsewhere_empty
  <chr>       <lgl>              <lgl>          
1 Fibroblasts TRUE               TRUE           
2 T_cell      TRUE               TRUE           
3 DCs         TRUE               TRUE           
rle(row_type)
Run Length Encoding
  lengths: int [1:3] 629 2200 4734
  values : chr [1:3] "DCs" "T_cell" "Fibroblasts"

Rows are grouped by cell type: dendritic cells, then T cells, then fibroblasts.

col_order <- names(mosaic)[order(match(col_type, cell_types))]

mosaic |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(v) !is.na(v)), cell = row_number()) |>
  pivot_longer(-cell, names_to = "variable", values_to = "has_value") |>
  mutate(variable = factor(variable, levels = col_order)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = cell, fill = has_value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_reverse() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "steelblue", `FALSE` = "grey90"),
                    labels = c(`TRUE` = "value", `FALSE` = "NA")) +
  labs(x = "variables (fibroblasts | T cells | dendritic cells)", y = "cells (rows of input.tsv)", fill = NULL,
       title = "The mosaic table uploaded to CausalCCC (case study 2)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

Variable names

In case study 1, a suffix (_senders, _receivers) was added only to genes measured on both sides. Here the rule looks similar but has gone wrong in places: some names carry the suffix twice. We split each name into its gene and its suffixes.

names_tbl <- tibble(variable = names(mosaic), cell_type = col_type) |>
  mutate(suffixes = str_count(variable, paste0("_(", paste(cell_types, collapse = "|"), ")")),
         gene     = str_remove_all(variable, paste0("_(", paste(cell_types, collapse = "|"), ")")))

Once the suffixes are removed, does a gene appear twice in the same cell type? If so, we compare the two columns on the cells of that type.

duplicates <- names_tbl |>
  group_by(cell_type, gene) |>
  filter(n() == 2) |>
  summarise(copy_1 = first(variable), copy_2 = last(variable), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(identical = pmap_lgl(list(cell_type, copy_1, copy_2), \(t, a, b) {
    identical(mosaic[[a]][row_type == t], mosaic[[b]][row_type == t])
  }))

14 genes appear twice in the same cell type, as two identical columns. For example S100A6_Fibroblasts and S100A6_Fibroblasts_Fibroblasts hold the same numbers, and so do ACTB and ACTB_T_cell. One copy has one suffix more than the other. The table was probably assembled from several sender–receiver runs, in which the same gene got different names (notebook 05, section 10). Section 7 shows what this does to the network.

The six discrete variables are the metadata: the cell subtype (labels_*, four subtypes per cell type, from the CellChat annotation) and the skin condition (condition_*: LS lesional or NL non-lesional skin of atopic dermatitis patients). Every gene is continuous.

mosaic |>
  mutate(cell_type = row_type,

  pivot_wider(names_from = condition, values_from = n)

Most dendritic cells and T cells come from lesional skin, while fibroblasts are more balanced.

4. The ligand–receptor pairs

The L-R pairs come from the CellChat analysis of this dataset (Jin et al., Nat Commun 2021). Each ligand and receptor name carries the cell type that expresses it, so we can read off the direction of each pair.

lr_pairs <- lr_pairs |>
  mutate(sender   = col_type[ligand],
         receiver = col_type[receptor])

count(lr_pairs, sender, receiver)

4 Fibroblasts T_cell          5

6 T_cell      Fibroblasts     5

lr_pairs |>
  summarise(all_ligands_ok   = all(ligand %in% state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "ligands"]),
            all_receptors_ok = all(receptor %in% state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "receptors"]))

The pairs cover all six directions between two different cell types; there is no autocrine pair (ligand and receptor in the same cell type). The pairs of Figure 3 (CXCL12 from fibroblasts to CXCR4 on dendritic cells and on T cells) are there.

How often is each ligand and receptor detected in its own cell type?

lr_genes <- unique(c(lr_pairs$ligand, lr_pairs$receptor))

lr_expression <- mosaic[lr_genes] |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "count") |>
  filter(!is.na(count)) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  summarise(fraction_detected = mean(count > 0)) |>
  mutate(role = if_else(variable %in% lr_pairs$ligand, "ligand", "receptor"))

ggplot(lr_expression, aes(x = fraction_detected, y = reorder(variable, fraction_detected), fill = role)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "cells of its own type where the gene is detected", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Detection of ligands and receptors") +
  theme_minimal()
lr_expression |> filter(fraction_detected < 0.1) |> arrange(fraction_detected)

  <chr>                         <dbl> <chr>

2 CD74_Fibroblasts             0.0792 receptor

5. The published network

We sort the retained links into categories using the cell type of each variable.

count(edges, type)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  type      n
  <chr> <int>
1 N      7743
2 P       715
network <- edges |>
  filter(type == "P") |>
  mutate(type_x   = col_type[x],
         type_y   = col_type[y],
         category = if_else(type_x == type_y, paste("within", type_x), "ligand-receptor"))

count(network, category)
# A tibble: 4 × 2
  category               n
  <chr>              <int>
1 ligand-receptor       43
2 within DCs           225
3 within Fibroblasts   247
4 within T_cell        200
# Number of cells used to learn each kind of link
count(network, category, cells_used = Nxy_ai)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  category           cells_used     n
  <chr>                   <dbl> <int>
1 ligand-receptor            NA    43
2 within DCs                629   225
3 within Fibroblasts       4734   247
4 within T_cell            2200   200

Links within a cell type are learnt from the cells of that type only; the 43 L-R links are given, not learnt (Nxy_ai is NA).

What MIIC reports for each link. Three levels of evidence, from weakest to strongest, should not be confused:

Level Column Meaning
Link present type = P the two genes are dependent, even after conditioning on the other genes
Oriented infOrt = 2 or -2 MIIC found a likely direction (x → y or y → x)
Genuine causation is_causal = Y MIIC considers the edge a genuine cause–effect relation; the paper draws it with a green arrowhead

Two other values of infOrt: 1 = not oriented, 6 = bidirected (a possible sign of a hidden common cause). A link can be oriented without being a genuine causation: this is the case of CXCL12 → CFD below. Most links are not oriented, and only a minority are genuine causations.

network |>
  mutate(orientation = case_when(infOrt ==  1 ~ "not oriented",
                                 infOrt %in% c(2, -2) ~ "oriented",
                                 infOrt ==  6 ~ "bidirected")) |>
  count(category, orientation) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = orientation, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
# A tibble: 4 × 4
  category           oriented bidirected `not oriented`
  <chr>                 <int>      <int>          <int>
1 ligand-receptor          43          0              0
2 within DCs               48          5            172
3 within Fibroblasts       82         33            132
4 within T_cell            58          6            136
count(network, is_causal)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  is_causal     n
  <chr>     <int>
1 N           666
2 Y            49

The metadata variables are part of the network. Their neighbours show which genes differ between subtypes or between lesional and non-lesional skin.

metadata_vars <- state_order$var_names[state_order$group == "metadata"]

6. Does the network support the paper’s description of Figure 3?

Figure 3C shows the “second-degree neighbourhood” of the two CXCL12–CXCR4 links: the genes at most two links away from CXCL12 in fibroblasts and from CXCR4 in dendritic cells and in T cells. The text names specific genes in that neighbourhood. We look for them in the network within each cell type, that is, without the L-R links, which would otherwise connect everything through the receptors.

intracellular <- network |> filter(category != "ligand-receptor")

Statement 1. CXCL12, secreted by fibroblasts, is linked to CXCR4 on dendritic cells and on T cells.

network |>
  filter(str_detect(x, "^CXCL12") | str_detect(y, "^CXCL12")) |>
  filter(category == "ligand-receptor") |>
  select(x, y, infOrt, proba)
# A tibble: 2 × 4
  x                  y            infOrt proba
  <chr>              <chr>         <dbl> <chr>
1 CXCL12_Fibroblasts CXCR4_DCs         2 0.5;1
2 CXCL12_Fibroblasts CXCR4_T_cell      2 0.5;1

Statement 2. Upstream of CXCL12 in fibroblasts: the fibroblast marker DCN and the adipose-related genes APOD and CFD.

The whole second-degree neighbourhood (to compare by eye with Figure 3C):

second_degree <- function(from) {
  d <- graph_distance(intracellular, from)
  d <- d[d <= 2]
  tibble(centre = from, gene = names(d), distance = d)
}

map(c("CXCL12_Fibroblasts", "CXCR4_DCs", "CXCR4_T_cell"), second_degree) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  filter(distance > 0) |>
  group_by(centre, distance) |>
  summarise(genes = paste(sort(gene), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop")

Figure 3B shows CXCL12 and CXCR4 expression in lesional skin. We draw the equivalent from the raw counts of the mosaic (on a log1p scale, i.e. log(1 + count)), separating lesional and non-lesional cells.

tibble(cell_type = row_type,
       condition = coalesce(mosaic$condition_Fibroblasts, mosaic$condition_T_cell, mosaic$condition_DCs),
       CXCL12    = mosaic$CXCL12_Fibroblasts,
       CXCR4     = coalesce(mosaic$CXCR4_DCs, mosaic$CXCR4_T_cell)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(CXCL12, CXCR4), names_to = "gene", values_to = "count") |>
  filter(!is.na(count)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = cell_type, y = log1p(count), fill = condition)) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width") +
  facet_wrap(~gene, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "log(1 + raw count)", fill = "skin",
       title = "CXCL12 in fibroblasts, CXCR4 in dendritic cells and T cells") +
  theme_minimal()

7. What do the duplicated columns do to the network?

Two identical columns carry the same information, so MIIC finds the strongest possible link between them.

duplicate_links <- link_name(duplicates$copy_1, duplicates$copy_2)

# Are the two copies of each duplicated gene linked to each other?
edges |>
  filter(link_name(x, y) %in% duplicate_links) |>
  count(type)

  filter(link_name(x, y) %in% duplicate_links) |>
  select(x, y, info_shifted, partial_correlation)

The 14 links between copies are the 14 strongest gene–gene links of their cell types, with a partial correlation of exactly 1. Since the L-R links are given the strength of the strongest link of the network, a duplicate also sets the strength of every L-R link.

Do the two copies of a gene have the same neighbours (apart from each other)?

intracellular_all <- network |> filter(category != "ligand-receptor")

duplicates |>
  mutate(neighbours = map2(copy_1, copy_2, \(a, b) {
    n_a <- setdiff(neighbors_of(a, intracellular_all)$neighbor, b)
    n_b <- setdiff(neighbors_of(b, intracellular_all)$neighbor, a)
    tibble(links_copy_1 = length(n_a), links_copy_2 = length(n_b), shared = length(intersect(n_a, n_b)))
  })) |>
  unnest(neighbours) |>
  select(cell_type, gene, links_copy_1, links_copy_2, shared)

   cell_type   gene     links_copy_1 links_copy_2 shared

10 T_cell      ACTB               15           15     15

12 T_cell      H3F3B               5            5      5
13 T_cell      S100A6              7            7      7
14 T_cell      SH3BGRL3            5            5      5

Each duplicated gene thus enters the network twice, with each neighbour linked to both copies: its links are counted twice, which inflates its importance as a hub. The two copies also count as two variables when MIIC looks for separating sets and for orientations. For the Figure 3 claims this matters little (none of the genes named in the text is duplicated), but it should be fixed when we rebuild the input.

What we learned

Inputs. The mosaic has 7,563 cells (4,734 fibroblasts, 2,200 T cells, 629 dendritic cells): the full CellChat data_humanSkin dataset, i.e. all cells of these three types from He et al. 2020. It has 238 variables: 232 genes (raw integer counts) and 6 discrete metadata (cell subtype and lesional/non-lesional skin, for each cell type). The 43 CellChat L-R pairs connect the three cell types in both directions.

Network. 715 links were kept out of 8,458 examined. The server needed about three hours, single-threaded.

Paper’s statements (Figure 3C). All supported, within the second-degree neighbourhood that the figure draws:

  • CXCL12 in fibroblasts is linked to CXCR4 in dendritic cells and in T cells (given L-R links).
  • CFD is a direct neighbour of CXCL12; DCN and APOD are two links away. Note that MIIC orients the link CXCL12 → CFD (not a genuine causation): CFD is on the fibroblast side, but the network does not put it upstream of CXCL12.
  • NR4A3 is a direct neighbour of CXCR4 in dendritic cells; GPR183 and VIM are two links away.
  • JUNB is a direct neighbour of CXCR4 in T cells; FOS is two links away.

The paper speaks of “upstream” and “downstream” genes. None of the links around CXCR4 is oriented, and the only oriented links of CXCL12 point away from it, so these words describe the position relative to the L-R link (sender side, receiver side) rather than a causal direction found by MIIC.

Points for the preprocessing assessment.

  • 14 genes appear twice in the same cell type as identical columns, under two names that differ by one suffix (S100A6_Fibroblasts / S100A6_Fibroblasts_Fibroblasts, ACTB / ACTB_T_cell, …). The link between two copies is the strongest of its cell type, and the gene’s links are counted twice (section 7).
  • Two L-R genes are detected in fewer than 10 % of the cells of their type: CCL19 (6 % of fibroblasts) and CD74 in fibroblasts (8 %).
  • Dendritic cells are few (629) and mostly from lesional skin: links within dendritic cells are learnt from fewer cells.
